'''''Salix cinerea''''' ('''common sallow''', '''grey sallow''', '''grey willow''', '''grey-leaved sallow''', '''large grey willow''', '''pussy willow''', '''rusty sallow'''<ref>{{cite web|title=Queensland Government Fact Sheet|access-date=24 April 2019|url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/salix_cinerea.htm}}</ref>) is a species of [[willow]] native to Europe and western Asia.<ref name=rdm>Meikle, R. D. (1984). ''Willows and Poplars of Great Britain and Ireland''. BSBI Handbook No. 4. {{ISBN|0-901158-07-0}}.</ref><ref name=kic>Christensen, K. I., & Nielsen, H. (1992). Rust-pil (''Salix cinerea'' subsp. ''oleifolia'') - en overset pil i Danmark og Skandinavien. ''Dansk Dendrologisk Årsskrift'' 10: 5-17.</ref>

The plant provides a great deal of [[nectar]] for [[pollinators]]. It was rated in the top 10, with a ranking of second place, for most nectar production (nectar per unit cover per year) in a [[United Kingdom|UK]] plants survey conducted by the AgriLand project which is supported by the UK Insect Pollinators Initiative.<ref name=Pollinators>{{cite web|title=Which flowers are the best source of nectar?|publisher=Conservation Grade|url=http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/|access-date=2017-10-18|date=2014-10-15|archive-date=2019-12-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191214024659/http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:2015-02-28 Close-ups of Salicaceae flowers, Weinviertel (Producer M. Stich).jpg|thumbnail|left|upright|Close-ups of Salicaceae flowers]]

It is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing 4–10 metres (13–30 ft) tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are spirally arranged, 2–9 cm (1–{{frac|3|1|2}} in) long and 1–3 cm ({{frac|1|2}}–{{frac|1|1|2}} in) broad (exceptionally up to 16 cm long and 5 cm broad), green above, hairy below, with a [[leaf#Margins (edge)|crenate]] margin. The [[flower]]s are produced in early spring in [[catkin]]s 2–5 cm long; it is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]] with male and female catkins on separate plants. The male catkins are silvery at first, turning yellow when the pollen is released; the female catkins are greenish grey, maturing in early summer to release the numerous tiny [[seed]]s embedded in white cottony down which assists wind dispersal.<ref name=rdm/><ref name=kic/>

==Taxonomy==
The closely related species ''[[Salix atrocinerea]]'' <small>Brot.</small>, which overlaps in distribution in [[France]], [[Belgium]], [[Netherlands]], [[England]] and [[Ireland]], is considered by some authors as the [[subspecies]] ''S. cinerea oleifolia'' <small>(Gaudin) Macreight</small>. '' S. atrocinerea'' differs from ''S. cinerea'' in that it is taller (reaching up to 15 metres), has a deeply furrowed bark, dark red-brown hairs beneath the leaves, smaller stipules, and is earlier deciduous.<ref name=rdm/><ref name=kic/> Despite the coexistence of these two nomenclatures, the main taxonomic databases regard ''S. cinerea oleifolia'' as synonym of ''S. atrocinerea''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Salix cinerea subsp. oleifolia (Gaudin) Macreight |website=Plant of the World Online|access-date=25 September 2024 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/77083742-1?_gl=1*haz52u*_ga*MjA2MDMzMDMyNS4xNzI1NTQ1MTI2*_ga_ZVV2HHW7P6*MTcyNzI1Njg3MS4zLjEuMTcyNzI1NjkyOC4wLjAuMA}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Salix atrocinerea Brot. |website=WFO Plant List|access-date=25 September 2024 |url=https://wfoplantlist.org/taxon/wfo-0000928979-2024-06?matched_id=wfo-0000931140&page=1}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Betula pubescens and Salix cinerea seeds.JPG|thumb|''Salix cinerea'' seeds on a birch tree branch]]
Grey willow grows in [[wetlands]], moist depressions, ditches, embankments, banks of stagnant or slow-moving water bodies, and forest edges, where it encounters low-lying damp situations with waterlogged and nutrient-poor soils. ''S. cinerea'' is a pioneer species that rapidly colonizes disturbed sites.<ref>Isebrands, J. G., & Richardson, J. (Eds.). (2014). Poplars and willows: trees for society and the environment. CAB International and FAO. {{ISBN|9781780641089}}</ref> 

A common herbivore of ''Salix cinerea'' is ''[[Phratora vulgatissima]]'', which prefers and is more common on female plants.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|title=Plant-sex-biased tritrophic interactions on dioecious willow|author=Kabir, Faisal MD|date=2015-04-19|journal=Ecosphere|volume = 5|issue = 12|pages = art153|doi=10.1890/ES14-00356.1|author2=Moritz, Kim K|author3=Stenberg, Johan A.|doi-access=free}}</ref> ''[[Anthocoris nemorum]]'', a natural enemy of ''Phratora vulgatissima'', is also more common on ''S. cinerea''.<ref name=":0"/>

==Invasive species==
''Salix cinerea'' is an [[invasive species]] in [[New Zealand]] and is listed on the [[National Pest Plant Accord]], which means it cannot be sold or distributed. ''S. cinerea'' is also highly invasive in south-eastern Australia,<ref>Cremer, K. W. (2003) Introduced willows can become invasive pests in Australia. Biodiversity, 4, 17-24.</ref> with the entire genus listed as a Weed of National Significance. The species was introduced to stop erosion along riverbanks, but has since caused worse erosion over time by widening and shallowing invaded streams.
